title: Token Minting
explain: To mint is to create something new under authority that others can recognise as genuine, usually with an expiry, like coins from a mint. The issuer signs, the verifier checks the signature, and a TTL or revocation ends it. Because a signed payload can be trusted without a database lookup, it lets you hand an otherwise untrusted object to a stranger.
model:
**Issuer signs -> verifier checks -> TTL / revoke.** (铸币厂: 只有它能造, 人人能验真, 有面值有效期.) Long-lived secrets stay home in the issuer; the outside world only receives **short-lived, verifiable, least-privilege** things.

Three questions for any mint (a good interview template):

1. **Who may mint?** (the authority holding the signing secret)
2. **How does a verifier check?** (signature alone, stateless; or lookup, stateful)
3. **How does it expire or get revoked?** (TTL, refresh, denylist, key rotation)

```
              Issuer (authority)
                  | mint
                  v
     token / key / ID / sequence number
          |           |            |
       verify       expire       revoke
   (signature/lookup) (TTL)      (denylist)
```

**What gets minted:** access tokens (JWT, STS credentials, pre-signed URLs, GitHub App tokens), keys and certs (KMS data key wrapped by a master key, short-lived mTLS certs), IDs (Snowflake, idempotency keys), and coordination numbers ([fencing token](#/sd/f/fencing-token), [lease](#/sd/f/lease), epoch/term; higher wins).

Fit for claims **fixed at issue time** that may be stale until expiry and that downstream needs. Signing is not encryption: the payload is readable. See [IdP](#/sd/f/idp).

details.q: Where does minting save a database hit?
details.a: Anywhere a verifier would otherwise ask 'is this allowed?': pre-signed S3 upload/download URLs (resource, method, expiry, signature), JWT access tokens (`user_id`, roles, `exp`), password-reset and email-verification links, CDN signed URLs and cookies, webhook signatures, CSRF tokens, capability tokens, job tokens (`job_id`, `attempt`, `worker_id`, `lease_expiry`). The verifier only checks the signature.

details.q: Which claims belong in a JWT access token that is checked only by signature?
details.a: Those fixed at issue time and acceptable if stale until `exp`: user id, scopes, expiry. Not a fast-changing value like an account balance, and never secrets or password hashes, since anyone holding the token can read the payload.

details.q: A service verifies JWTs locally with a 15-minute lifetime and an account is banned. How quickly is the user cut off?
details.a: When the token expires, up to 15 minutes. That is the statelessness trade-off: verification needs no database and so cannot see revocations. For faster effect add a small denylist or session-version check on sensitive endpoints, and keep TTLs short with refresh tokens.

details.q: Forty microservices verify tokens signed with HMAC-SHA256 using one shared secret. One is compromised. Risk?
details.a: The attacker can mint valid tokens for any user and scope, because verifying and minting use the same secret. Use asymmetric signing: the issuer holds the private key, verifiers hold only the public key and can check but never forge.

details.q: Signing keys rotate from key A to key B at 12:00 and tokens last 1 hour. How long must verifiers still accept A?
details.a: About 60 minutes: the last token signed with A was issued just before 12:00 and expires just before 13:00. Retire A earlier and valid tokens suddenly fail. Identify keys by a `kid` header and publish the key set.

details.q: What is the order of a stateless bearer-token verification?
details.a: Parse the token and read `kid` and claims; fetch (or use a cached copy of) the issuer's public key; verify the signature; check `exp`, `nbf`, issuer and audience; only then authorise using the scopes. Never use claims before the signature has been verified.

details.q: A KMS `GenerateDataKey` returns a plaintext key and the same key encrypted under a master key. Which principle is that?
details.a: The master key never leaves the issuer; it mints small one-off keys that do the work. The app encrypts with the plaintext key, stores the encrypted key beside the data and discards the plaintext, and only the issuer can unwrap it later. Same shape as a JWT signer and its tokens.

prompts.q: Explain minting with the three questions you would ask of any mint.
points: Who may mint (authority holds the signing secret)
How a verifier checks (signature vs lookup)
How it expires and is revoked (TTL, refresh, denylist, rotation)
Short-lived and least-privilege outward, long-lived secret stays home

prompts.q: When is a minted token the right tool, and what does it cost?
points: Saves a DB hit; can be given to a stranger
Claims fixed at issue time and acceptable if stale
Signing is not encryption: no secrets in the payload
Revocation is the cost of statelessness: short TTL, denylist

prompts.q: Compare HMAC and asymmetric signing for many verifiers, and describe key rotation.
points: HMAC: every verifier can also mint
kid header and a published key set
Keep the old key until the last token expires
